plan.title: The Pomodoro Technique: Focus in 25-Minute Bursts
plan.description: The Pomodoro technique splits work into 25-minute focus sessions separated by short breaks. Learn how it works, why it helps, and how to start today.

beats.narration: You sit down to work, and an hour later you have checked your phone ten times and written two sentences. What if the fix was a kitchen timer shaped like a tomato?

In the late 1980s, a university student named Francesco Cirillo struggled to concentrate. He grabbed a tomato timer and challenged himself to focus for just a few minutes. Pomodoro is Italian for tomato.
The big idea is simple. Do not try to focus all day. Focus hard for one short, fixed block of time, then rest. That is the whole technique.

props.text: Focus hard for one short block, then rest.

beats.narration: Here is the method. First, pick one task. Second, set a timer for twenty-five minutes. Third, work on nothing else until it rings. Fourth, take a five-minute break.
Put together, the cycle is this. Work 25 minutes. Then a short break of 5 minutes. Repeat four times, and after the fourth round, take a longer break.
If a distraction pops into your head mid-session, do not act on it. Jot it on a piece of paper and go back to work. It will still be there at your break.

beats.narration: Why does a tiny timer help? Starting is the hardest part of any task, and twenty-five minutes feels small enough to begin. Once you start, momentum often carries you.
Three things make it work. A small, easy start lowers resistance. Built-in urgency keeps your attention sharp. And visible progress, one finished Pomodoro after another, feels rewarding.
It is not magic, and it is not rigid. If your work needs longer stretches, such as deep writing, adjust the lengths. The point is a focused block followed by a real rest.
So today, pick one task, set a timer for twenty-five minutes, and give it everything. One focused tomato at a time is how big work gets done.
